perspective:
I, Carolyn Abebe, have access to the following:

- I am Carolyn Abebe, a Black woman, a bank teller with a bachelor’s degree.
- Marilyn Olson is my colleague at the community bank; we recently started working together, and I respect her.
- During a busy week at the bank, I noticed Marilyn was unusually quiet and withdrawn, unlike her normally engaging demeanor.
- I asked Marilyn if everything was alright and if she wanted to talk. She told me she was overwhelmed with work and some personal stuff, and thanked me for asking.
- Later, I perceived Marilyn as responding curtly. I felt confused and slightly hurt. I told her I hoped I hadn’t overstepped, shared that I’d had tough times too, and said talking can sometimes help. Marilyn said she appreciated that, apologized if she seemed off, and said it had been a hard week.
- Marilyn appeared to respond positively to my openness. I felt relieved and hopeful about our friendship. I invited her to a small weekend get-together, and she accepted.
- Despite friendly interactions outside work, I felt Marilyn was still keeping a professional distance at the bank. I felt disappointed and asked to talk about our work dynamic. Marilyn said she hadn’t realized that, apologized if it seemed that way, and agreed to talk about improving collaboration.
- After our private meeting, I believed we had cleared the air and better understood each other’s professional expectations and personal boundaries. I felt content and optimistic.
- I proposed that Marilyn and I team up on the new project proposal. She agreed, said she was glad we had talked, and said she looked forward to working more closely with me.

I do not have access to Marilyn’s private thoughts, unspoken reasons for her behavior, or any information she did not tell me or show through her actions.
